title: Monitoring, Logs and Debugging

header.html: Use built-in CLI tools to monitor Kubernetes applications; Utilize container logs; Debugging in Kubernetes
Kubernetes v1.37.0 (3-node test cluster, containerd 2.3.4, Metrics Server v0.9.0)

toc.title: A debugging routine that works every time

html:
1A debugging routine that works every time

Start with the status, and let it tell you where to look. Do these in order and stop when you find the cause.

Step Command What it tells you
1. Status k get pods -o wide the STATUS word, READY, RESTARTS, the node
2. Events k describe pod <pod> (read the Events at the bottom) why scheduling, pulling or starting failed
3. Logs k logs <pod> (-c, --previous) what the app itself said
4. Inside k exec -it <pod> -- sh the app's view: files, DNS, network
5. Cluster events k get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp the newest events of the namespace

What the status word tells you

STATUS Usual cause Where to look
Pending no node fits (CPU or memory request too big, taint, unbound PVC, unmatched node selector) describe Events: "0/3 nodes are available ..."
ContainerCreating (long) volume or secret problem, slow image pull describe
ErrImagePull, ImagePullBackOff wrong image name or tag, private registry without a pull secret describe
CreateContainerConfigError a referenced ConfigMap, Secret or key does not exist describe
CrashLoopBackOff the process exits with an error again and again logs --previous
Error / OOMKilled exit code not zero / memory limit exceeded describe (Last State), logs
Init:0/1, Init:Error an init container is not finished logs -c <init-container>
Running but 0/1 Ready readiness probe failing describe, get endpoints
Terminating for ever finalizer or a stuck volume describe; last resort delete --force --grace-period=0

2Container logs

k logs web                       # one container Pod
k logs web -c sidecar            # pick a container (needed when there are several)
k logs web --all-containers      # every container, one after the other
k logs web --previous            # the container instance before the last restart
k logs web --tail=20             # last 20 lines
k logs web --since=10m           # only the last ten minutes
k logs web -f                    # follow (Ctrl+C to stop)
k logs -l app=web --prefix       # all Pods with a label, prefixed with the Pod name
k logs deploy/web                # one Pod of a Deployment
k logs job/batch                 # the Pod of a Job

Logs are what the container wrote to standard output and standard error. An app that writes to a file inside the container (not to stdout) has no kubectl logs: read the file with exec, or add a sidecar that tails it (Module 3). Logs of a deleted Pod are gone; a crashed container's previous log is kept only for the last restart.

Save logs to a file on the exam host with the shell redirect: k logs web -c worker --tail=3 > ~/answers/worker-tail.txt. kubectl logs prints a "Defaulted container ..." note to stderr when a Pod has several containers and you did not choose one, and it then reads the first container: read the task carefully for the container name.

3Resource usage: kubectl top

kubectl top needs the Metrics Server (installed on the cluster; if top says "Metrics API not available", it is missing or still starting).

k top nodes                              # CPU and memory per node
k top pods -n load                       # per Pod
k top pods -A --sort-by=cpu              # the biggest CPU users first
k top pods --sort-by=memory --no-headers | head -1   # the top memory user, no header line
k top pod web --containers               # per container

CPU is in millicores (250m is a quarter of a core); memory is in Mi. The numbers are a recent average and take about a minute to appear for a new Pod. They show use, not the requests or limits you set (those are in describe).

4Getting inside and moving data

k exec web -- ls /etc/app                   # one command
k exec -it web -c main -- sh                # a shell in a container
k exec web -- cat /etc/app/version > ver.txt   # read a file out, redirect on the exam host
k cp web:/var/log/app.log ./app.log -c main    # copy a file out (needs tar in the container)
k port-forward pod/web 8080:80              # localhost:8080 on your machine reaches Pod port 80
k port-forward svc/web 8080:80              # through a Service
k run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- sh   # a throw-away Pod for tests
k get pod web -o yaml                       # the live object, including status
k get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=web

Ephemeral debug containers. Many images have no shell (distroless, pause). You cannot exec into them, and a Pod's containers cannot be added after creation. kubectl debug attaches a temporary container with the tools you want to a running Pod, sharing its network and, with --target, its process space:

k debug tiny --image=busybox:1.36 --target=tiny --container=dbg -- sh -c "sleep 3600"
k debug -it tiny --image=busybox:1.36 --target=tiny    # interactive shell
k debug web --copy-to=web-debug --image=busybox:1.36 -- sleep 3600   # a copy of the Pod, original untouched
k debug node/<name> -it --image=busybox:1.36           # a Pod on a node, node file system under /host

An ephemeral container is listed in spec.ephemeralContainers, is not restarted, and cannot be removed; delete the Pod when you are done.

5Typical faults and the fix

Symptom Fix
CrashLoopBackOff, log says a setting is missing add the env, ConfigMap or Secret the log names (k set env deployment app KEY=value)
CreateContainerConfigError for a ConfigMap create the ConfigMap with the exact name and key that describe shows
ImagePullBackOff correct the image name or tag: k set image deployment web nginx=nginx:alpine
Pending: "Insufficient cpu" lower the request (Pod: delete and recreate; Deployment: edit)
Pods 0/1 Ready fix the readiness probe path or port, or the app
Service without endpoints the Service selector must match the Pod labels (Module 14)
Exam tip

. Do not guess: run k describe pod and read the last five lines. The Events almost always name the cause. Then change one thing and verify.

Exam tip

. A Deployment's Pods are replaced when you change the template, so edit the Deployment. A bare Pod's resources, image pull policy and most spec fields cannot be edited: export the YAML, change it, delete and recreate.

6Lab tasks

<!-- LABS: m08 -->

Lab 8.1: logs one container

Domain: Observability | Points: 5 | Time: about 5 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-01-logs-one-container)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The Pod shop in the namespace dbg has two containers, web and worker. Write only the last 3 lines of the log of the container worker to ~/answers/worker-tail.txt on the host where you run kubectl.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dbg logs shop -c worker --tail=3 > ~/answers/worker-tail.txt
cat ~/answers/worker-tail.txt

Lab 8.2: crashloop env

Domain: Observability | Points: 7 | Time: about 8 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-02-crashloop-env)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace dbg, the Pod of the Deployment app keeps crashing (CrashLoopBackOff). Read the container log to find the cause and fix it without changing the image or the command: the application needs the environment variable DB_URL with the value postgres://db:5432/app. Wait until the Deployment has 1 Ready replica.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dbg get pods
kubectl -n dbg logs deploy/app --tail=5
kubectl -n dbg set env deployment app DB_URL=postgres://db:5432/app
kubectl -n dbg rollout status deployment app --timeout=120s

Lab 8.3: top pods

Domain: Observability | Points: 5 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-03-top-pods)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace load, three Pods are running and the cluster has the Metrics Server. Find the Pod that uses the most CPU right now with kubectl top and write only its name to ~/answers/top.txt on the host where you run kubectl.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n load top pods
kubectl -n load top pods --sort-by=cpu --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{print $1}' > ~/answers/top.txt
cat ~/answers/top.txt

Lab 8.4: ephemeral debug container

Domain: Observability | Points: 7 | Time: about 8 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-04-ephemeral-debug-container)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The Pod tiny in the namespace dbg runs an image that has no shell, so you cannot exec into it. Without recreating the Pod, attach an ephemeral debug container named dbg (image busybox:1.36, targeting the container tiny) that runs sh -c "echo debug-ok > /tmp/dbg.txt; sleep 3600". The Pod must stay Running.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dbg debug tiny --image=busybox:1.36 --target=tiny --container=dbg -- sh -c "echo debug-ok > /tmp/dbg.txt; sleep 3600"
for i in $(seq 1 30); do kubectl -n dbg get pod tiny -o jsonpath='{.status.ephemeralContainerStatuses[0].state.running}' | grep -q startedAt && break; sleep 2; done
kubectl -n dbg exec tiny -c dbg -- cat /tmp/dbg.txt

Lab 8.5: exec read files

Domain: Observability | Points: 5 | Time: about 5 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-05-exec-read-files)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The Pod files in the namespace dbg runs a container named main. Without changing the Pod: write the content of the file /etc/app/version inside the container (just the text) to ~/answers/version.txt, and write the number of lines of the file /var/log/app.log inside the container (just the number) to ~/answers/lines.txt, both on the host where you run kubectl.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dbg exec files -c main -- cat /etc/app/version > ~/answers/version.txt
kubectl -n dbg exec files -c main -- wc -l /var/log/app.log | awk '{print $1}' > ~/answers/lines.txt
cat ~/answers/version.txt ~/answers/lines.txt

Lab 8.6: fix pending pod

Domain: Observability | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-06-fix-pending-pod)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The Pod big in the namespace dbg (manifest ~/work/big.yaml) stays Pending. Find the reason in its events and fix the manifest so that the Pod is Running: lower the CPU request to 100m. Keep the name, image and namespace. A Pod's resources cannot be edited in place, so recreate it.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dbg describe pod big | tail -5
kubectl -n dbg delete pod big --wait=true
sed -i 's/cpu: "100"/cpu: 100m/' ~/work/big.yaml
kubectl apply -f ~/work/big.yaml
kubectl -n dbg wait --for=condition=Ready pod/big --timeout=120s

Lab 8.7: missing configmap

Domain: Observability | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m08-07-missing-configmap)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace dbg, the Pod of the Deployment svc does not start (CreateContainerConfigError). Find the cause with kubectl describe, and fix it without changing the Deployment: create what is missing so that the Deployment has 1 Ready replica. The application expects LEVEL=info from that source.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dbg describe pod -l app=svc | grep -i -A3 "Events"
kubectl -n dbg create configmap app-config --from-literal=LEVEL=info
kubectl -n dbg rollout status deployment svc --timeout=120s

<!-- /LABS -->

7Recall questions

R1Which command shows the log of the previous container instance?

Show the answer

kubectl logs <pod> --previous.

R2How do you read the log of one container of a multi-container Pod?

Show the answer

kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>.

R3What does Running with 0/1 READY mean?

Show the answer

The container runs but its readiness probe fails (or the app is not ready).

R4Which component must exist for kubectl top to work?

Show the answer

The Metrics Server.

R5How do you list Pods by memory use, the largest first?

Show the answer

kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory.

R6Which command attaches a temporary tools container to a running Pod?

Show the answer

kubectl debug <pod> --image=<image> --target=<container>.

R7What does CreateContainerConfigError usually mean?

Show the answer

A ConfigMap, Secret or key that the Pod references does not exist.

R8Where do you read why a Pod is Pending?

Show the answer

In the Events at the end of kubectl describe pod.

Quick Reference Card

Topic Remember
Routine get (status), describe (events), logs (-c, --previous), exec
Logs stdout and stderr only; --tail, --since, -f, -l, --all-containers
top Metrics Server; --sort-by=cpu|memory, --containers; millicores and Mi
debug ephemeral container (--target), --copy-to, node/<name>
Data exec ... > file, cp, port-forward
Statuses Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerConfigError, CrashLoopBackOff, 0/1 Ready
Fix location Deployment: edit it; bare Pod: delete and recreate
